title: Chapter I
focus: Nick, the Eggs and the Buchanans

teacherSummary.text: Nick Carraway, a Yale graduate from a well-off Midwestern family, explains that he came East in 1922 to learn the bond business and rented a small house in West Egg beside Gatsby's mansion. He dines across the bay in East Egg with his cousin Daisy, her husband Tom Buchanan (a former Yale football star with a 'cruel body') and the golfer Jordan Baker. Tom rants about a racist book; a phone call reveals that Tom has a mistress; Daisy tells Nick she hopes her daughter will be 'a beautiful little fool.' Back home, Nick sees Gatsby alone on his lawn, stretching his arms toward a green light across the water.

context.history: Great Neck and Manhasset Neck on Long Island's North Shore were home to new show-business fortunes and old society families in the early 1920s; Fitzgerald lived in Great Neck in 1922–24. After the First World War many young men from the Midwest moved east to work in finance, as Nick does.

significance: The opening establishes Nick as both guide and suspect witness, maps the novel's class geography (West Egg versus East Egg), and plants its key symbol, the green light.

segments.script: Great Neck and Manhasset Neck on Long Island's North Shore were home to new show-business fortunes and old society families in the early 1920s; Fitzgerald lived in Great Neck in 1922–24. After the First World War many young men from the Midwest moved east to work in finance, as Nick does. The opening establishes Nick as both guide and suspect witness, maps the novel's class geography (West Egg versus East Egg), and plants its key symbol, the green light. Point of view: Nick introduces himself as a narrator "inclined to reserve all judgements," then judges everyone; the reader must weigh his claims. Setting: West Egg (new money, Nick's "eyesore" and Gatsby's mansion) faces East Egg (old money, the Buchanans) across the bay. Characterization: Tom's "cruel body," Daisy's thrilling voice and despairing irony, Jordan's balanced boredom. Watch for the green light: Gatsby, alone at night, stretches his arms toward "a single green light, minute and far away."

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I’ve been turning over in my mind ever since” slowly and put it in my own words: Nick recalls advice from his father that he has kept turning over in his mind since he was young. Next, craft. I notice he presents himself as thoughtful and impressionable, "younger and more vulnerable," before telling us anything else. The strongest word is “vulnerable”: it shows he wants to seem open and easily hurt, which makes us trust him. Then, effect. What does Nick want us to think about him from his father's advice? My answer: From his father's advice, Nick wants us to think of him as a fair, reserved judge who is slow to criticize others; the novel will test whether that self-image is true.
